newsitem.title: USA: US T-bond yld eyes 6.5 pct by yr-end, 6 pct in '97.
newsitem.headline: US T-bond yld eyes 6.5 pct by yr-end, 6 pct in '97.

text.p: Long-term U.S. interest rates could drop to 6.50 percent before 1996 comes to a close in a bid to crack the critical 6.0 percent barrier next year, economists and analysts said on Wednesday.
Yields on the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond dropped to 6.64 percent early Wednesday, their lowest level in nearly seven months, before rebounding slightly in the late morning.
Bond prices, which move in the opposite direction of their yields, soared two full points in Tuesday's session, chalking up their biggest one-day gain in about 16 months.

"We are probably headed below 6.50 percent by the end of this year, and we could go as low as 6.0 percent by the end of 1997," said Michelle Colley Laughlin, Treasury market strategist at Prudential Securities Inc. "I think we'll see a move toward a sustained slowing of economic activity."
Monetary and fiscal policy remains tight, Laughlin said, while consumer attitudes are sluggish at best. Similarly, pent-up consumer demand hardly abounds.
Meanwhile, a fervent U.S. dollar could undermine exports, and the overall pattern for growth is historically slow in the year following a presidential election, she added.
"All these factors could lead to a more sustained economic slowdown in 1997," Laughlin said. "We could even raise speculation of a recession."
Prudential Securities, according to Laughlin, expects the Federal Reserve to ease credit policy by the end of 1997.

The central bank last altered the overnight bank lending, or federal funds rate, on January 31 when it trimmed it by 25 basis points. Fed funds rate have since stood at 5.25 percent, while the more symbolic discount rate rests at 5.0 percent.
In addition, Prudential predicts growth will slow to a mere 1.0 percent by the second half of next year.
"It will mostly be very positive news (for the Treasury market) about the economy" that will drive long-term rates lower next year, the Prudential strategist added.
Experts were less sure, however, that the T-bond next year could tackle its all-time record low of 5.77 percent reached just over three years ago.

The 5.77-percent level marks the lowest point for the 30-year security since the Treasury began issuing 30-year paper on a regular basis in 1977. However, the 30-year issue was not always auctioned regularly prior to that time and it was not always non-callable as it is today.

Thus, analysts say the 10-year note is a better historical reference for long-term interest rates prior to 1977. In mid-October of 1993, the yield on the 10-year note dropped to 5.17 percent, the lowest level since July of 1967.
In mid-morning trade on Wednesday, the 10-year yield stood at 6.40 percent, compared to 6.70 percent one month ago and just about 7.0 percent at mid-year.
Over the more immediate term, Michael Krauss, managing director and chief technical strategist at Chase Securities Inc, said the long bond's performance depends on how the market finishes the month.
"It depends on how we close the month and the week," Krauss said. "If we close above 6.68 (percent), I'd be looking for something around 6.53 and maybe 6.47 percent."
To the upside, Krauss said he expects the bond yield to bump up against resistance at around 6.73 and 6.80 percent.
Krauss, agreed with Laughlin, noting that if a sustained sea-change prevails and the economy indeed weakens further, bonds will benefit.
However, he said the belly of the Treasury yield curve might be the real winner. "The bond is not the asset of choice right now," he said.
Krauss predicted funds would flow from other fixed income sectors -- mainly corporates and mortgages -- as well as equities, to boost the intermediate sector of the yield curve.
